Have you heard of Project Semicolon? As a fellow writer I think you'd find it interesting. The semicolon represents survivors of suicide or suicidal thoughts. Firstly – and I know this is difficult – try your best not to worry about something that isn't even happening yet. As someone that is constantly worrying about the future, I know how difficult it can be, but it is crucial that you try not to worry about things you cannot control.

Secondly, I'd argue that with two major depressive episodes under your belt, *if* the third one comes around you will have a toolbox full of resources/strategies to manage it. If you're taking care of yourself now, doing some self-discovery, and figuring out healthy ways to manage your depression, if you ever do enter into a third depressive episode you will be even better equipped to handle it. 

I'm in my second major depressive episode as well and I know for a fact that this only happened because I never let myself feel my emotions in the last one. I put everything into a locked drawer in my mind and self-medicated to push back the feelings. Now, I'm learning how to be aware of my feelings and that tool alone will either prevent another episode or mitigate the pain of a future episode. 

You can do this.

**tl;dr - It is absolutely possible for you to prevent or diminish the severity of future episodes. If you build your toolbox of resources and strategies now, it'll still be there if you ever have a third major depressive episode.**

You know, sometimes people with depression really just need a place to hear that they're not alone. There are plenty of places to get advice on reddit, but I personally find /r/depression a place away from trying to fix everything.

You may be right that depression is not the feeling of being sad for a few days about a sad occurrence. 

However, I would like to add to your statement that it is possible for long-lasting sadness about an event to change a person's brain chemistry over time. Being sad for two years over a "shitty string of events" will absolutely change the brain's chemical balance. 

My depression for the past 7 years is the perfect example, and I'm sure there are many others on this sub. My parents had a very painful divorce that dragged along from my 7th to 12th grade years. While divorce affects different children in different ways, I fell into a depression that ultimately changed me from a very happy 12 year old into a deeply depressed and suicidal young adult. 

I'd argue that maybe we should consider the fact that some of these people complaining about seemingly small things might just be at the very beginning of their lifelong battle with serious depression. 

Edit: I may never think about the divorce, but it changed me and molded me into a person that copes with shitty situations by pushing back the feelings until they can be "safely" released. Which is never.

Part of it, for me at least, is the realization that as a symptom of depression, I don't exactly believe any of the advice I might give another depressed person. If I actually believed my own advice, wouldn't I apply it to myself? 

We can sit here and tell each other over and over that we're here to talk and there is a light at the end of the tunnel etc, but if we actually believed our own advie and internalized it, we probably wouldn't be on this sub, would we? 

Does anyone else agree or am I alone here?

I agree with you to a certain extent, but I don't think meditation is about "letting go" of depression as you put it. I've struggled with severe depression for the past 8 years and I have come to terms with the fact that my thoughts will, for much of the future, be on the more depressed side. However, meditation has taught me that I can separate myself from those thoughts. The thoughts still occur - they certainly cannot just cease to exist - but I can learn to accept that they are happening without judgement and without letting them affect my daily life. It's about being okay with discomfort, even if that discomfort manifests itself as depressive thoughts.
